**Course source:** Day 1 §3.1. **Running system:** Order, Product, and User services.

## Why a service name is better than a fixed address

Order needs Product. But Product could have instances at ports 4101 and 4104 today, then a different IP tomorrow. Hard-coding those addresses inside Order makes every deployment a coordination task.

A **registry** keeps service-instance records such as a logical name, host, port and optional health information. A provider registers or is registered by infrastructure; a consumer discovers one or more candidates and then chooses where to send a request.

~~~text
Product A ----register----> Registry <----lookup---- Order
Product B ----register---->    |                       |
                               +----instance list------+
~~~

Registration and discovery are separate: an instance being present in the registry does not guarantee its next HTTP request will succeed. A failed node can remain listed until its lease or health state expires.

## Push or pull discovery

In *client-side discovery*, Order obtains instances and chooses one (the course later uses Ribbon). In *server-side discovery*, Order sends to a stable name or proxy and the proxy selects the instance. Both still need a source of current endpoint information.

A discovery client may cache records to avoid a registry lookup on every call. This improves performance but creates staleness windows. After a Product crash, Order might briefly choose the dead instance.

## Practical design checks

Evaluate service identity, lease duration, removal behaviour, split-brain behaviour, security of registration and whether the registry itself is highly available. Do not point every request at one registry server without considering failure.

The original course compares Eureka and Consul. Kubernetes deployments can instead resolve service names through platform DNS and Services, depending on operational requirements. Discovery is a **capability**, not necessarily a separate tool.

## Test your reasoning

Name the component that owns this responsibility, explain its behaviour during a failure, and identify one configuration or metric you would verify in production.
